question: Explain price elasticity of demand. Illustrate your answer with an example.

rubric.name: Definition
rubric.description: States PED as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price (percentage/proportionate method).

rubric.name: Application
rubric.description: Applies the concept correctly with numbers or a concrete example, distinguishing elastic (>1) from inelastic (<1) demand.

rubric.name: Interpretation
rubric.description: Explains what elasticity implies: responsiveness, its determinants (substitutes, necessity), or a pricing/revenue implication.

responses.text: Price elasticity of demand measures the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. If a 10% price rise cuts demand for movie tickets by 20%, PED = 2, which is elastic. Necessities like salt are inelastic since demand barely changes.
PED is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price.
If price increases by Rs 10 and demand falls by 50 units, then elasticity is 50 units.

PED = %change in Qd / %change in P. It shows how responsive buyers are to price. Luxury goods like branded shoes are elastic (PED above 1) because people can postpone or switch; medicines are inelastic since patients must buy anyway.
When Maggi price increased people shifted to Yippee, showing demand is elastic for such products.

It is the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price, measured in percentage terms. Example: if petrol price rises 10% and demand falls only 2%, elasticity is 0.2, inelastic, because there are few substitutes.
Price elasticity of demand is the law that when price increases demand decreases and when price decreases demand increases.
Elasticity of demand means how much demand changes when price changes, calculated in percentage terms.

Elasticity of demand = percentage change in demand / percentage change in price. A value above 1 means elastic, e.g. restaurant meals, where a small price hike makes many customers cook at home. Below 1 is inelastic, like electricity.
Elasticity is simply the change in quantity: when the price of a pen rose by 2 rupees, demand fell by 30 pens, so PED = 30.
PED tells us by what percent demand changes when price changes by one percent. Cold drinks: a 5% price rise and 15% demand fall gives PED 3, highly elastic because Pepsi can replace Coke easily.
It is %ΔQd / %ΔP. Elastic goods have elasticity more than 1.
For salt, even if price rises we buy the same amount. For an AC, if price rises a lot fewer people buy. This difference between goods is elasticity.

Defined as percentage change in quantity demanded over percentage change in price. Salt is the classic inelastic example: even if price doubles, families buy nearly the same amount, so revenue rises when price rises.
Elasticity is the slope of the demand curve; a steeper demand curve always means more elastic demand.

It measures sensitivity of demand to price in percentage terms. Elastic (above 1): demand changes more than price, like air travel for tourists. Inelastic (below 1): less than price, like insulin. Firms use it to set prices.
Price elasticity = proportionate change in demand over proportionate change in price. Example: luxury goods.
%ΔQ / %ΔP. Suppose a phone brand raises price 8% and sales drop 16%: PED = 2, elastic, so the price rise reduces revenue. That is why competitive goods rarely raise prices.
PED = fall in demand divided by rise in price = 40 units / Rs 5 = 8.
Formula is percentage change in demand upon percentage change in price. I don't remember the interpretation part.

Price elasticity of demand is how much quantity demanded responds to price changes, in percentages. Example: a 20% discount raising ice-cream sales by 60% gives PED of 3; substitutes and non-necessity make it elastic.
Elasticity means demand and price move in opposite directions. Example: price up, demand down. That is what elasticity states.
PED measures responsiveness of demand to price. Formula: %change in Q divided by %change in P.

The ratio of proportionate change in quantity demanded to proportionate change in price. Textbook example: wheat is inelastic as it is a staple; designer bags are elastic because buyers can delay purchase.
If a 10% fee hike makes many students leave a coaching class, its demand is elastic. Didn't write the formula.
PED = percentage fall in demand / percentage rise in price. If bus fare rises 10% and ridership falls 5%, PED is 0.5, inelastic since commuters have few options. So the transport company earns more.
Elasticity means how many units of demand change per rupee change in price, like 15 units per rupee.
It is the ratio of % change in quantity demanded to % change in price of the good.

It quantifies buyer responsiveness: %change in Qd divided by %change in P. Cinema tickets in a city with many OTT options are elastic; life-saving drugs are inelastic. This interpretation guides pricing power.
Petrol demand doesn't fall much when price rises because we need it daily. That means inelastic demand.

Measures percentage change in quantity demanded per percentage change in price. Elastic demand (above 1) means total revenue falls when price rises; inelastic (below 1) means revenue rises. Raising milk price slightly won't cut sales much.
A flatter line has less elasticity because slope is small; elasticity and slope are basically the same thing.
Elasticity shows sensitivity of consumers to price, found by dividing percent change in demand by percent change in price.

PED shows the strength of the law of demand in percentage terms: how strongly quantity reacts. Gold jewellery is elastic since purchases are postponable, matchboxes are inelastic being a cheap necessity with a tiny share of income.
Elasticity of demand tells how flexible demand is with respect to price. Higher elasticity means demand is more flexible.
The bigger the drop in units sold, the bigger the elasticity. If sales drop 500 units it is highly elastic no matter the price.

Percentage method: PED = (%ΔQd)/(%ΔP). A 10% rise in coaching fees reducing enrolments by 25% gives 2.5, elastic, because students can switch institutes. Institutes with unique results face lower elasticity.
It indicates whether demand is sensitive or not sensitive to price. Sensitive means elastic and not sensitive means inelastic.
PED is percentage change in price divided by percentage change in quantity demanded, so if price changes 10% and quantity 20%, elasticity is 0.5.

It's the degree of responsiveness of demand to a price change, measured by comparing percentage changes. E.g. a 4% price rise with a 2% demand fall gives 0.5, inelastic; happens for necessities with no close substitutes.
Demand responsiveness to price change is called elasticity; it depends on substitutes and the nature of the good.
PED = %ΔQ/%ΔP. If price changes 5% and quantity changes 10%, PED = 2.

Elasticity = %change in demand ÷ %change in price; sign ignored. Above 1 elastic, exactly 1 unitary, below 1 inelastic. Example: onions are surprisingly inelastic in India since meals need them regardless.
PED explains the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded as per the demand curve.
%change in quantity / %change in price. Eg 20%/10% = 2.
PED tells the degree to which price affects the demand of a commodity in the market.
Elasticity = (ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔP/P). For 100 to 90 units when price goes 50 to 55, it is (-10%) ÷ (10%) = -1, take absolute value 1, unitary.

PED compares the % change in units demanded to the % change in price. Example: OTT subscription price up 15%, subscribers down 30%, PED = 2, elastic due to many rival platforms; the firm should reconsider the hike.
Using the percentage method: quantity falls 8% when price rises 4%, so elasticity is 2 for this good.

It measures how the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in its price, expressed as the ratio of percentage changes. Example: a 10% rise in taxi fares cutting rides 18% gives PED 1.8; riders switch to the metro, so demand is elastic.
